section.title: The Angel at Bochim
section.sectionRationale: After the long catalogue of compromise in chapter 1, heaven speaks. The Angel of the LORD comes up from Gilgal, where the conquest began, to Bochim and delivers a covenant lawsuit: I kept My word, you broke yours. The verdict is that the very nations Israel refused to drive out will now remain as thorns and their gods as a snare. The people weep and offer sacrifice, and the place is named Weepers. It is one short, weighty movement, the divine interpretation of the failure just described.
section.thesis: The Angel of the LORD confronts Israel's broken covenant, holding His own faithfulness against their disobedience, and pronounces that their unfinished obedience will become their ongoing snare; the people grieve, yet grief that names the place Weepers is not the same as repentance that turns.
section.frameNote: Two beats: the Angel's covenant indictment and sentence, verses 1 to 3; and the people's weeping and sacrifice at Bochim, verses 4 to 5.

units.label: The Angel's covenant lawsuit
units.note: I kept My word, you broke yours

verses.text: Now the {{malak|angel}} of the LORD went up from Gilgal to Bochim and said, “I brought you up out of Egypt and led you into the land that I had promised to your fathers, and I said, ‘I will never break My {{berith|covenant}} with you,
and you are not to make a covenant with the people of this land, but you shall tear down their altars.’ Yet you have not obeyed My voice. What is this you have done?
So now I tell you that I will not drive out these people before you; they will be thorns in your sides, and their gods will be a snare to you.”

units.label: The people weep at Bochim
units.note: grief that names the place Weepers

verses.text: When the angel of the LORD had spoken these words to all the Israelites, the people lifted up their voices and {{bakah|wept}}.
So they called that place {{bochim|Bochim}} and offered sacrifices there to the LORD.

malak.gloss: Messenger or angel. The Angel of the LORD speaks in the first person as the God who brought Israel out of Egypt and made the covenant, so many readers understand this as a unique appearance of the LORD Himself, a foreshadowing of the Son who reveals the Father. The BSB footnote allows the capitalized Angel.

berith.gloss: Covenant, a binding bond sworn between the LORD and His people. The Angel's speech is a covenant lawsuit: God kept His side, I will never break My covenant with you, while Israel broke theirs by making a covenant with the peoples of the land instead of tearing down their altars.

bakah.gloss: To weep, cry aloud. When the people hear the indictment they lift up their voices and weep. The word captures real sorrow, yet the narrative that follows shows this grief did not become lasting repentance; they wept over the consequences without turning from the sin.

bochim.gloss: Weepers, the name given to the place, from the same root as the verb to weep. Where the conquest had begun at Gilgal, Israel now marks a place of tears; the very naming preaches that the era opens not in triumph but in mourning.

basic.context: This short scene is the hinge between the failures listed in chapter 1 and the cycle described later in chapter 2. The Angel of the LORD travels up from Gilgal, the place where the conquest under Joshua had begun, to a place that will now be called Bochim, Weepers. He speaks like a prosecutor in a covenant court: I kept every promise, but you disobeyed by sparing the Canaanites and leaving their altars standing. Because of that, He says, I will no longer drive these nations out; they will be thorns in your sides and their gods a snare. The people burst into tears and offer sacrifices. The question hanging over the scene is whether their weeping will turn into real, lasting change, and the rest of the book gives a sobering answer.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative carrying a strong theological message; it interprets the compromise of chapter 1 as covenant unfaithfulness, not mere military shortfall. We should read the Angel's words as a genuine indictment and a just sentence, and the people's tears honestly, as real emotion that nonetheless stops short of repentance. The passage is not prescribing that we tear down literal altars today; it presses the deeper principle that partial obedience is disobedience, and that God takes His covenant, and its breach, with full seriousness.
basic.originalLanguages: The scene opens with the malak, the Angel or messenger, of the LORD, who speaks in the first person as the God of the exodus and covenant. His speech is a berith, covenant, lawsuit: He kept His bond, Israel broke theirs. When they hear it the people bakah, weep aloud, and the place is named bochim, Weepers, from the same root. The very name of the place becomes a sermon: the era begins in tears.
basic.typology: The Angel of the LORD who comes up to confront and yet still receives sacrifice foreshadows Christ, in whom God draws near to a covenant-breaking people both to indict sin and to provide atonement. Bochim, a place of weeping over sin met by sacrifice, points toward the greater sorrow and the greater sacrifice at the cross, where true tears of repentance find a Lamb who actually takes sin away.
basic.christ: The Angel of the LORD speaks with the authority of God Himself, the God who kept every promise while His people broke theirs. That gap between God's faithfulness and human faithlessness is the whole problem the gospel answers. At Bochim Israel weeps and sacrifices, but the tears do not last and the sacrifices cannot change the heart. Jesus is the faithful covenant partner Israel could never be, and He is the true sacrifice that turns weeping into cleansing. He weeps over hard-hearted cities Himself, and then bears the covenant curse we deserved so that our grief over sin can become godly sorrow that leads to life.
basic.god: God is shown to be perfectly faithful, I will never break My covenant with you, and this makes Israel's unfaithfulness all the more striking. He is patient, coming to explain and to warn rather than to destroy. He is just, allowing the consequences of Israel's own choices, the nations they spared, to become the thorns and snares they will now live with. And He is still approachable in mercy, receiving sacrifice from a weeping people even as He pronounces the hard word.
basic.crossReferences: Joshua 5 records the conquest beginning at Gilgal, the very place the Angel now leaves behind. Numbers 33 warned that spared nations would become barbs in Israel's eyes and thorns in their sides. Second Corinthians 7 distinguishes godly sorrow that leads to repentance from worldly sorrow that leads to death. And Hebrews 12 warns against tears that come too late, like Esau's.
basic.oneStory: Bochim is the moment God tells Israel what their compromise means: the unfinished conquest is a broken covenant, and the enemies they kept will now keep them. The people weep but do not truly turn, and the whole book unfolds from this unhealed sorrow. It leaves us longing for the faithful One who keeps the covenant on our behalf and whose sacrifice turns mere weeping into true repentance, Jesus, God come near to save.

context.literary:
These five verses are shaped as a classic covenant lawsuit, the same legal-prophetic form later prophets will use at length: a recital of the LORD's saving acts in the first person, I brought you up, I led you, I said, followed by direct quotation of the covenant obligation Israel broke, you are not to make a covenant, you shall tear down their altars, then a piercing rhetorical question that functions as an indictment, what is this you have done, and finally an announced sentence, I will not drive out. Later prophets use this identical four-part shape at greater length, Isaiah 1:2-20 and Micah 6:1-5 among them, which suggests the narrator of Judges is deliberately borrowing courtroom language his first hearers would recognize from Israel's later worship and preaching.

The passage also pivots on a change of speaker and register. Verses 1 to 3 are entirely first-person divine speech, urgent and unbroken; verses 4 to 5 drop into flat third-person narration, the people lifted up their voices and wept, as though the narrator steps back once the verdict lands and simply records the human response without commentary or resolution.

Geography frames the whole scene. The unit opens at Gilgal, Israel's first camp after the Jordan and the base from which the conquest under Joshua was launched, and closes at a place that receives, for the first time in the text, the name Bochim. The move from an old name marking triumph to a brand new name marking grief is the chapter's structure in miniature.
context.historical:
Gilgal was no ordinary campsite. It was where the twelve memorial stones from the Jordan crossing stood, Joshua 4:19-24, where the nation was circumcised anew and kept its first Passover in the land, Joshua 5:2-10, and where the manna ceased the very day they ate the produce of Canaan, Joshua 5:12; it functioned as Israel's ongoing base of covenant renewal throughout the conquest. For the Angel of the LORD to depart from that place and travel to a location the text has not previously named signals a genuinely new moment, not a return to routine.

The text does not say where Bochim lay, and nothing should be invented about its location; what can be said with confidence is that Canaanite worship in this period centered on open-air high places, stone altars, and standing pillars, often marked by a sacred pole or Asherah image, sites that dotted hilltops across the land the tribes had just failed to fully clear. Moses had commanded that these very structures be torn down rather than merely ignored, because in the ancient world a standing altar was not a neutral ruin but an active point of contact, a place where sacrifice, oath, and allegiance were still being transacted. Leaving Canaanite altars standing, then, was never a passive oversight; it left live channels open for exactly the worship the Angel now names as covenant treachery.
context.canonical:
The covenant lawsuit form heard here becomes a favorite prophetic vehicle later in the canon, most fully in Isaiah 1:2-20, where heaven and earth are summoned as witnesses, and in Micah 6:1-5, where the LORD again recites His saving acts before charging His people with ingratitude; readers who know those later chapters hear in Bochim an early, compact rehearsal of the same divine courtroom.

This is also one of several places across Scripture where the Angel of the LORD appears carrying full divine authority, alongside His visits to Hagar, Genesis 16:7-13, to Abraham at the sacrifice of Isaac, Genesis 22:11-12, to Moses at the burning bush, Exodus 3:2-6, and to Joshua before Jericho as commander of the LORD's army, Joshua 5:13-15; across these appearances the Angel both speaks with God's own voice and is treated as worthy of reverence, a consistent pattern this scene extends rather than departs from.

Bochim's tears also have an earlier canonical parallel worth noticing. When the spies' report frightened Israel out of entering the land, the people wept all that night, Numbers 14:1, and then, told the door was now shut, presumed to march up anyway without the LORD's presence, and were routed, Numbers 14:39-45; weeping that changed nothing about the heart led straight into further disaster. Bochim's tears risk exactly the same pattern, and the rest of Judges shows they did.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
By placing this scene immediately after the long tribal catalogue of chapter 1 and immediately before the theological overview that opens in verse 6, the narrator uses Bochim as the hinge that forces a specific interpretation onto everything just read: the tribes' failures were not simply military shortfalls or hard providence, they were a broken oath, and the narrator wants no reader to mistake compromise for circumstance. By having the Angel quote Israel's own covenant obligation back to them almost verbatim, tear down their altars, rather than paraphrasing it, the author denies his hearers any excuse that they had forgotten the actual terms; the terms are restated in full before the verdict falls.

The author also intends the scene to explain why the land, rather than growing safer with time, would instead grow more dangerous, since the very nations left standing were now formally declared future thorns rather than temporary nuisances. And by ending the unit on a place name that means Weepers rather than on any note of restored obedience, the writer leaves the tension of the whole book unresolved at its outset: real grief has occurred, but nothing yet shown proves it reaches the root.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The scene records one specific confrontation between the Angel of the LORD and a specific covenant nation at a specific moment in redemptive history; it is not a manual for how modern believers are meant to identify and physically destroy the religious structures of neighboring peoples, a task nowhere assigned to the church, whose weapons are not of this world. What transfers directly is the pattern beneath the history: covenant obligations that are only partly kept are, in God's own accounting, simply broken, not half honored, and consequences that look like circumstance, difficult neighbors, ongoing temptation, a hostile culture, may in fact be the outworking of an earlier compromise rather than bad luck. The scene also gives readers a diagnostic question to ask of their own emotion: does this sorrow move toward the altar of confession and change, as true repentance must, or does it stop at tears over consequences, satisfied merely to have felt something before returning to the same road.

debates.question: Who is the Angel of the LORD who speaks here?

views.label: A created angel bearing God's message
views.case: The word malak simply means messenger, and prophets and angels regularly speak God's words in the first person as His mouthpiece; on this view the Angel delivers the LORD's covenant lawsuit as His authorized representative, without being God Himself.

views.label: A unique appearance of the LORD Himself
views.case: The speaker claims to have brought Israel up from Egypt and to have sworn the covenant, and he receives sacrifice, things proper to God alone; the BSB footnote even allows the capitalized Angel, and many read this as a pre-incarnate appearance of the Son who makes God known.

debates.bearing: Either way the words carry full divine authority; and the second reading enriches the scene, showing God Himself drawing near both to indict His people and, at Bochim, to receive their sacrifice, a foretaste of the God who comes near in Christ.

debates.question: Was the weeping at Bochim true repentance?

views.label: Genuine but shallow repentance
views.case: The people are cut to the heart, weep aloud, and offer sacrifices to the LORD, all marks of real conviction; at that moment their sorrow appears sincere, even if it did not endure.

views.label: Regret over consequences, not the sin
views.case: The very next section of the chapter shows the people plunging into the cycle of idolatry with no lasting change; their tears seem to mourn the announced thorns and snares rather than the covenant-breaking that caused them, worldly sorrow rather than godly.

debates.bearing: The distinction is pastorally vital: Scripture calls for sorrow that turns from sin, not merely sorrow that laments its cost, and Bochim stands as a warning against mistaking feeling for repentance.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond the four words already named, the passage's Hebrew repays attention in three further places. The charge itself, you have not obeyed My voice, uses the common verb for hearing, the same root that opens Israel's daily confession, Hear, O Israel, the LORD our God, the LORD is one, Deuteronomy 6:4. In Hebrew, obedience is grammatically indistinguishable from hearing; there is no separate word for compliance that does not first mean listening. To say Israel did not obey is, in the language itself, to say Israel stopped truly hearing, which explains why the Angel's whole speech is built as something spoken aloud rather than merely commanded once and filed away.

The accusing question in verse 2, what is this you have done, belongs to a small, recognizable family of confrontational questions that recur across the Torah and beyond, nearly word for word to the LORD's question to the woman in the garden, Genesis 3:13, and to Abimelech's rebuke of Isaac, Genesis 26:9-10, with looser cousins in Pharaoh's protest to Abram, Genesis 12:18, Joseph's test of his brothers, Genesis 44:15, and the sailors' demand of Jonah, Jonah 1:10. Each instance catches someone in a moment of exposed wrongdoing that they cannot argue their way out of; by placing the same formula in the Angel's mouth, the narrator quietly aligns Israel's covenant breach with Eve's first act of distrust, the oldest sin now repeating itself on a national scale.

The verb behind will never break, describing the LORD's own faithfulness, belongs to a family of Hebrew words used elsewhere for the violent snapping of something previously whole, a covenant, a yoke, a staff, rather than a quiet lapse or forgetting; when the same root appears negated of God, it insists that His side of the bond could not simply come undone by neglect the way Israel's has. And the place name Bochim, coming from the same root as the verb to weep just used of the people, functions the way many Hebrew place names do throughout the historical books, freezing a single moment of national experience into permanent geography, so that travelers passing through would go on asking what happened here long after the generation that wept had died.

typology.type: The Angel who both recites grace and pronounces the verdict, Judges 2:1-3
typology.fulfillment: In the wilderness the Angel of the LORD had already gone ahead of Israel bearing the divine name itself, listen to his voice, Exodus 23:20-21, and now the same figure returns to hold Israel to the terms of a journey He led in person. John later writes that no one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son has made Him known, John 1:18, and Hebrews describes the Son as the exact representation of God's nature, Hebrews 1:3, the same pattern of a divine messenger who is somehow also the LORD Himself carried to its full clarity. Christ likewise both recounts covenant grace, this is My blood of the covenant, Matthew 26:28, and still holds His hearers to an account nothing can evade.

typology.type: The formula what is this you have done, echoing Eden, Judges 2:2
typology.fulfillment: The same accusing question once put to the first woman is put here to an entire nation, tying Israel's covenant breach back to humanity's oldest sin, distrust that edits God's word down to something more manageable. Paul later warns a whole church that it could be led astray just as Eve was deceived by the serpent's cunning, 2 Corinthians 11:3, treating Genesis 3 as a template for every community's slide from simple devotion. Christ is the last Adam who, tested with the same kind of question, answers instead with unwavering trust in what is written, Matthew 4:4, reversing at last the pattern Bochim only repeats.

typology.type: Bochim, weeping over sin that still receives sacrifice, Judges 2:4-5
typology.fulfillment: The people's tears do not close the scene; sacrifice follows, a sign that atonement, however provisional under the old covenant, was still being offered even to a people caught freshly in covenant breach. The gospel answers this pairing of grief and offering with a sorrow that actually reaches its goal, godly sorrow that brings repentance without regret, 2 Corinthians 7:10, met by a sacrifice that does not merely accompany tears but genuinely reconciles, since through Him we have now received reconciliation, Romans 5:11. What Bochim only pictures in shadow, an accused people still allowed to bring an offering, the cross secures in substance.

typology.type: The journey from Gilgal, where a reproach was rolled away, to Bochim, the place of tears, Judges 2:1
typology.fulfillment: Gilgal itself was named for a reproach the LORD had already rolled away, Joshua 5:9, so the Angel's short journey traces Israel's whole spiritual arc in two syllables of geography, from disgrace removed to disgrace renewed within a single generation. Scripture elsewhere follows the same arc in reverse at the cross, where the place of ultimate reproach, Golgotha, becomes the very ground from which believers now go out bearing a different disgrace altogether, Hebrews 13:12-13. Bochim is not the last word for God's people any more than Gilgal's old name was; the pattern of shame met and answered keeps recurring until Christ.

study.christ:
The Angel's whole complaint turns on a single failure: Israel did not obey My voice. That phrase becomes one of the most important in all of Scripture once the Gospels open, because a voice from heaven authenticates Jesus at a decisive turning point of His ministry, this is My beloved Son, listen to Him, Mark 9:7, and the Father's own testimony rests entirely on whether people will finally do what Bochim's generation did not, actually listen. Hebrews later contrasts the two eras directly: in the past God spoke through the prophets, but in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son, Hebrews 1:1-2, and warns that if the message spoken through angels was binding, how much more urgent is it not to neglect a salvation announced by the Lord Himself, Hebrews 2:2-3. Bochim's Angel delivers one covenant word Israel had already broken; the Son delivers a covenant word believers are warned never to drift past.

The scene's unresolved ending, tears and sacrifice with no stated word of forgiveness, also throws the finished work of Christ into relief. Nothing in the text tells us the LORD accepted the offering at Bochim or that the sentence in verse 3 was lifted; the narrative simply moves on, and the rest of Judges shows the thorns arriving exactly as promised. The New Testament, by contrast, does not leave that question hanging: when we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness, 1 John 1:9, a certainty Bochim's worshipers had no way to claim for themselves. And where the Angel's message could only diagnose Israel's condition, not change it, the Son's own promise reaches further still: a new covenant not like the one made with their fathers, a covenant they broke, in which God puts His law in their minds and inscribes it on their hearts, Jeremiah 31:31-33, the very obedience Bochim's generation could not sustain, finally supplied from within rather than merely announced from without.
study.god:
Notice who moves first in this scene. Before Israel says a single word, the Angel of the LORD has already gone up, already spoken, already recited grace before naming failure; nothing in the passage suggests Israel initiated this encounter by seeking God out. That order matters for how the whole of Scripture describes the relationship between God and His people: He is consistently the one who comes looking, who speaks before He is spoken to, and who indicts sin not from a distance but by drawing near to it, a pattern that will recur when the Word Himself comes and dwells among a people who, on the whole, do not receive Him, John 1:11.

God is also willing to keep talking to a people He already knows will not fully change. Nothing in His opening recital of grace or His closing sentence suggests naivety about how this will turn out; the God who says these words is the same God whose knowledge spans every age, and yet He still delivers the confrontation in full rather than silently withdrawing or striking without warning. Judgment, in other words, is never wordless in Scripture; it comes with an accounting a person or nation could, in principle, still answer rightly.

Finally, God allows His own confrontation to be memorialized in the very landscape His people will walk through afterward. Bochim becomes a fixed point on the map, and every future traveler who asks what the name means is handed, without any sermon required, the whole story of a covenant broken and mourned. This is a God who lets His dealings with His people become embedded in geography and memory rather than vanishing once the moment passes, the same instinct behind Israel's memorial stones at Gilgal and, further on, behind the church's own ongoing practice of remembering, do this in remembrance of Me, Luke 22:19. A God who could simply have let the thorns grow up in silence instead chooses, at the very first opportunity, to name what has happened and why, refusing to let His people mistake ordinary hardship for a fate that fell on them by chance.

crossReferences.note: God had already warned through Moses, long before Israel entered the land, that any inhabitants left in place would become barbs in their eyes and thorns in their sides, harassing them in their own territory. The sentence pronounced at Bochim, they will be thorns in your sides, quotes this warning almost word for word, showing the Angel is not improvising a punishment but simply enforcing terms Israel had heard decades earlier.

Gilgal was named for a reproach the LORD rolled away there, and it became Israel's staging ground for the whole conquest under Joshua. The Angel's departure from that very place to confront Israel's covenant breach traces, in a single verse, the distance a generation can travel from a rolled-away disgrace back into a fresh one.

Paul distinguishes godly sorrow, which produces repentance leading to salvation without regret, from worldly sorrow, which produces death. Bochim's weeping sits exactly on that fault line, and the rest of Judges answers which kind of sorrow it actually was by showing the nation slide back into the same idolatry within a single generation.

Esau sought the blessing he had traded away with tears, yet found no ground for repentance though he sought it. His grief, like Bochim's, was real and yet arrived too entangled with the consequences of his choice to reverse it, a sober warning that tears alone, however sincere, do not automatically undo what careless choices have already set in motion.

What is this you have done, asked first of the woman in the garden after she ate the forbidden fruit, is nearly the exact question the Angel now puts to an entire nation. The repetition ties Israel's national covenant breach to humanity's very first act of distrust, suggesting the fall in Eden and the failure at Bochim spring from the identical root.

An earlier generation also mourned bitterly on hearing a hard word from the LORD, then presumed to march up into the land anyway without His presence, and was routed. Bochim's tears risk the same shallow pattern, grief over a verdict rather than genuine repentance, and Judges will go on to show that this second generation fell into a version of the very danger the first one did.

Israel's central daily confession begins with the command to hear, using the same root the Angel uses to charge Israel with not obeying His voice. In Hebrew, obedience and hearing share one word, so the accusation at Bochim is, at bottom, that Israel had stopped truly listening to the confession it recited.

In the past, the writer says, God spoke through the prophets in many times and ways, but in these last days He has spoken by His Son. The Angel's single confrontation at Bochim is one instance of exactly that older pattern of partial, occasional divine speech, which the New Testament says has now been surpassed by a final and complete word.

Centuries later Micah reuses the same courtroom shape heard at Bochim, the LORD reciting His saving acts, I brought you up from the land of Egypt, before pressing His covenant lawsuit against Israel. The prophet's fuller indictment shows how deeply this five-verse scene at Bochim had already established the pattern Israel's later prophets would use again and again.

study.oneStory:
Every promise God had made since Eden depended on His own word holding, and Bochim is the first moment in Israel's story in the land where that word is set explicitly against a nation's covenant breach in open court. The scene functions as a small, compressed rehearsal of themes that stretch across the whole Bible: a rescued people forgetting rescue, a Redeemer who still comes looking, an accusation the guilty cannot answer, and a response of grief that history alone can judge as shallow or deep.

Bochim also marks a hinge in the land's own moral geography. Before this scene, unfinished conquest could still be read as an unfortunate military shortfall; after it, every remaining Canaanite enclave carries a name, thorns, and a purpose, testing, so that the map of the land becomes a theological document as much as a political one. Every future judge, every future oppressor named in the chapters ahead, steps onto ground the LORD has already explained here in advance.

The weeping at Bochim also anticipates a tension the rest of Scripture keeps working out: that emotion is not the same as obedience, and that God takes no pleasure in sorrow which changes nothing. The prophets will press the same distinction for centuries, calling for a rending of hearts rather than garments, Joel 2:13, until the New Testament finally supplies what Bochim's generation lacked, a Spirit who does not merely move people to tears but writes God's law on the heart itself, so that grief over sin and the power to turn from it arrive together rather than one without the other. Bochim leaves its readers with real tears and an unanswered question; the gospel is the answer that scene could not yet give, tears met by a change that lasts.

quiz.q: What is the heart of the Angel of the LORD's message at Bochim?

options.text: God kept His covenant faithfully, but Israel broke theirs by sparing the Canaanites and their altars.
options.note: Verses 1 to 2 are a covenant lawsuit: God's faithfulness set against Israel's disobedience.

options.text: God is angry that Israel lost too many battles.
options.note: The issue is not military failure as such but covenant unfaithfulness, disobeying God's voice.

options.text: God announces He is abandoning Israel entirely.
options.note: He pronounces consequences and even receives sacrifice; He does not abandon them outright.

options.text: God praises Israel for completing the conquest.
options.note: The opposite: He indicts them for leaving the conquest unfinished.

quiz.q: What consequence does the Angel pronounce?

options.text: The nations Israel spared will remain as thorns in their sides, and their gods will be a snare.
options.note: Verse 3 states the sentence, fulfilling the earlier warning of Numbers 33.

options.text: Israel will be sent back into slavery in Egypt.
options.note: A return to bondage is not the sentence here; the spared nations becoming thorns and snares is.

options.text: The land will be struck with famine.
options.note: The specific consequence named is the remaining nations and their gods, not famine.

options.text: Nothing at all will change for Israel.
options.note: A real and lasting consequence is announced; the era of thorns and snares begins here.

quiz.q: What does the name Bochim mean, and why does it matter?

options.text: It means Weepers, marking that the era opens in mourning rather than triumph.
options.note: Verse 5 and the footnote give the meaning; the name itself preaches the tragedy.

options.text: It means Victory, celebrating Israel's conquest.
options.note: This inverts the meaning; the name marks tears, not victory, the very point of the scene.

options.text: It is simply an old place name with no significance.
options.note: The narrator draws attention to the name precisely because it carries meaning.

options.text: It means the Canaanites had repented.
options.note: It refers to Israel's weeping, not to any Canaanite repentance.

quiz.q: How should we understand the people's weeping at Bochim?

options.text: As real emotion that stopped short of lasting repentance, since they soon returned to idolatry.
options.note: The following verses show no lasting change, exposing sorrow over consequences rather than sin.

options.text: As deep and genuine repentance that changed the nation.
options.note: The tears were real, but the book immediately shows the change did not last.

options.text: As mere play-acting with no feeling at all.
options.note: The grief was sincere in the moment; the failure was that it did not turn them from sin.

options.text: As unnecessary, since they had done nothing wrong.
options.note: They had broken covenant; the weeping was a response to a real and just indictment.

questions: The Angel held God's faithfulness against Israel's failure. Where has God kept His word to you even where you have not kept yours to Him, and how does that move you?
God said the nations Israel spared would become thorns and snares. What tolerated compromise in your life has quietly become a source of pain you now live with?
The people wept but did not truly turn. How can you tell the difference in your own heart between sorrow over consequences and genuine repentance?
The scene moves from Gilgal, the place of victory, to Bochim, the place of tears. Are there areas where your walk with God has drifted from triumph to mourning, and what would returning look like?
Jesus kept the covenant we could not and became the sacrifice our tears could never provide. How does resting in His faithfulness change the way you come to God with your failures?

translationNotes.note: The angel of the LORD may be rendered the Angel of the LORD, as the BSB footnote allows; the speaker uses the first person of God's own saving acts, which many take to signal a unique appearance of the LORD Himself.
Thorns in your sides and their gods will be a snare echo the earlier warning of Numbers 33:55; the imagery describes tolerated enemies and idols that will wound and entangle Israel from within.
Bochim means Weepers, as the BSB footnote notes; the place is named for the people's response, tying the name to the verb to weep in verse 4.
